q: Under the step-ladder (step) method of secondary distribution of overheads:

options.A: Service departments serve each other repeatedly until the residual balances become negligible
options.B: The costs of service departments are ignored altogether
options.C: All service departments are apportioned simultaneously by means of simultaneous equations
options.D: The service departments are arranged in a sequence and apportioned one after another, a department once closed receiving no further apportionment

q: A predetermined overhead absorption rate, based on budgeted overheads and the budgeted level of the absorption base, is used mainly because:

options.A: It gives the exact actual cost of each job executed
options.B: It enables jobs to be costed promptly without waiting for the actual overheads, and avoids wide fluctuations in unit cost from month to month
options.C: It eliminates the need for preparing budgets
options.D: It guarantees that the overheads will be exactly absorbed

q: Under absorption costing, the closing stock of finished goods is valued at:

options.C: Full cost of production, including a share of fixed production overheads
options.D: Selling price less selling and distribution expenses

q: The basic reason why the profit under absorption costing differs from the profit under marginal costing is that:

options.A: Fixed production overheads are carried forward in the value of closing stock under absorption costing, whereas under marginal costing they are charged in full against the profit of the period
options.B: Variable costs are measured differently under the two methods
options.C: Selling overheads are ignored under marginal costing
options.D: Depreciation is not charged under absorption costing

q: A product sells for Rs 150 per unit. Its variable cost per unit is: material Rs 50, labour Rs 30 and variable overheads Rs 20. Fixed costs are Rs 2,00,000 and 8,000 units are sold. The profit under marginal costing is:
A product sells for Rs 250 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 150 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 3,60,000. The break-even sales value is:
The margin of safety of a business can be improved by:

options.A: Increasing sales volume, reducing fixed costs or reducing the variable cost per unit
options.B: Increasing the fixed costs of the business
options.C: Reducing the selling price without any change in costs or volume
options.D: Increasing the break-even point of the business

q: In break-even analysis, when the margin of safety (in sales value) and the P/V ratio are known, the profit is computed as:

options.A: Margin of safety multiplied by total fixed costs
options.B: Margin of safety divided by the P/V ratio
options.C: Total sales multiplied by the P/V ratio
options.D: Margin of safety multiplied by the P/V ratio

q: The P/V ratio of a firm is 50% and its fixed costs are Rs 3,60,000. The sales required to earn a profit equal to 20% of sales are:
If the selling price of a product is increased while its variable cost per unit and total fixed costs remain unchanged, the break-even point will:

options.B: Decrease, because the contribution per unit increases

q: Raw material is the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 90 per unit and consumes 3 kg of material per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 120 per unit and consumes 5 kg of material per unit. Production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product A, because its contribution per kg of material (Rs 30) is higher
options.B: Product B, because its contribution per unit is higher
options.C: Product B, because it consumes more material per unit

q: A factory has 9,000 kg of a scarce material. Product A requires 3 kg per unit, gives a contribution of Rs 90 per unit and has a maximum demand of 2,000 units. Product B requires 5 kg per unit and gives a contribution of Rs 100 per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:

A component is required in 10,000 units per year. Making it in-house involves a variable cost of Rs 24 per unit and specific fixed costs of Rs 30,000 per year, which would be wholly avoided if the component were bought. An outside supplier offers it at Rs 30 per unit. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Buy, because the purchase price is recovered from the customers in the selling price
options.B: Make, because the total relevant cost of making (Rs 2,70,000) is less than the cost of buying (Rs 3,00,000)
options.C: Buy, because the supplier's price of Rs 30 per unit is a firm quoted price
options.D: Remain indifferent, as the two alternatives cost the same

q: Which of the following is a qualitative (non-financial) factor in a make-or-buy decision?

options.A: The variable cost of making the component
options.B: The purchase price quoted by the outside supplier
options.C: The degree of control the firm retains over the quality and timely supply of the component
options.D: The fixed costs that will continue even if the component is bought

q: A firm has spare capacity. Its variable cost is Rs 48 per unit. It receives a one-time special order for 3,000 units at Rs 55 per unit, involving no extra fixed cost. The order should be:

options.A: Accepted, because it adds Rs 21,000 to the profit of the firm
options.B: Rejected, because the price offered is below the normal selling price
options.C: Accepted only if the price is raised to cover the full cost per unit
options.D: Rejected, because special orders reduce the margin of safety

q: When a firm is already working at full capacity, a special order should be accepted only if its price covers:

options.A: The variable cost of the order alone
options.B: The variable cost plus an equal share of the fixed costs
options.C: Only the direct material cost of the order
options.D: The variable cost plus the contribution that would be lost on the regular work displaced by the order

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 3,00,000 per year, of which Rs 1,20,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown. The contribution is Rs 45 per unit. The shutdown point is:
In deciding whether to shut down a plant temporarily during a period of very low demand, the relevant comparison is between:

options.A: The total cost of the plant and its total revenue
options.B: The loss if the plant is operated and the loss if it is shut — the latter consisting of the unavoidable fixed costs plus the costs of closing down and of re-opening
options.C: The fixed costs and the variable costs of the plant
options.D: The book value of the plant and its market value

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 15 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 14 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 3,000 kg. The material price variance is:

options.A: The budgeted fixed overheads and the actual fixed overheads incurred
options.B: The fixed overheads absorbed and the budgeted fixed overheads
options.C: The budgeted output and the actual output of the period
options.D: The standard hours and the actual hours worked

q: In process costing, an abnormal gain arises when:

options.A: The actual output of the process is less than the input
options.B: The scrap of the process realises more than its expected value
options.C: The cost of the process exceeds the budgeted cost
options.D: The actual loss in the process is less than the normal loss expected, so that the actual output exceeds the expected output; the gain is valued at the cost per unit of good output

q: A by-product, as distinguished from a joint product, is a product which:

options.A: Is the main product for the manufacture of which the process is run
options.B: Arises incidentally in the course of manufacturing the main product and is of relatively small sales value
options.C: Always has no sales value and must necessarily be scrapped
options.D: Is necessarily produced in a separate subsequent process

options.A: Are performed for each individual unit produced, such as machining
options.B: Support the factory as a whole, such as plant management and security
options.C: Are performed for each product line, such as product design and engineering
options.D: Are performed each time a batch is processed — such as machine set-ups, first-item inspection and materials movement — regardless of the number of units in the batch

q: A proposed project requires land already owned by the enterprise, which could alternatively be sold for Rs 2,00,000. In appraising the project, this amount of Rs 2,00,000 should be:

options.B: Treated as a cost (cash outflow) of the project, being its opportunity cost
options.C: Treated as a benefit of the project
options.D: Recorded only in the notes to the accounts

options.A: The salvage value of the plant and the recovery of the working capital invested in the project
options.B: The depreciation charged in the final year of the project
options.C: The initial cost of the project
options.D: The book value of assets scrapped without any sale

q: Where a number of projects are independent of each other and there is no shortage of funds, the correct capital budgeting decision is to accept:

options.A: Only the project with the highest internal rate of return
options.B: Only the project with the shortest payback period
options.C: Only one project, whichever is the cheapest
options.D: All projects with a positive net present value

q: If an enterprise uses the same overall weighted average cost of capital as the discount rate for appraising all projects, irrespective of the risk of each project, the likely consequence is that it may:

options.A: Accept some high-risk projects that destroy value and reject some safe, worthwhile projects

options.A: The book value of the machinery
options.C: Only the profit earned on the sale

options.D: An increase in funds from operations

options.A: Additional earnings from the work plus savings in working expenses expected from it, after deducting the additional working expenses
options.B: Only the additional earnings from new traffic
options.C: Only the savings in working expenses

options.A: Can never be sanctioned in any circumstances
options.B: Is sanctioned automatically if any State Government supports it
options.C: May still be sanctioned on strategic or developmental considerations, its justification then resting on economic rather than purely financial returns
options.D: Must be executed only through a public-private partnership concession

options.D: Comptroller and Auditor General of India

options.A: The inputs consumed by a programme
options.B: The physical outputs produced by a programme
options.C: The final results and impact of the expenditure on the intended beneficiaries, rather than merely the outputs produced

options.A: Budgets are prepared with the active involvement of the managers who will be responsible for achieving them, which generally improves motivation and commitment to the targets
